subject: health
title: Healthy Bodies, Healthy Routines
standards: Michigan Health Practice 5: Self-Management and Goal Setting
Michigan Health Practice 3: Information and Resource Seeking
Michigan Health Topic (Grades 3-5): Personal Health and Wellness
essential_question: How do everyday routines keep my body well and stop germs from spreading?

topic_content.name: daily hygiene routines
key_points: A routine is a set of steps you do in the same order, so you do not have to remember each one separately.
Morning usually includes washing face and hands, brushing teeth, and dressing for the weather.
Evening usually includes washing, brushing teeth, and getting to bed at a steady time.
Routines work better when they are attached to something that already happens, like brushing right after breakfast.
topic_content.scenario: Sam keeps forgetting to brush in the morning because the family leaves in a rush. Where in Sam's morning could brushing be attached so it is harder to forget?

topic_content.name: handwashing and how germs spread
key_points: Germs are far too small to see, and hands look clean even when they carry them.
Germs move by touch, by coughs and sneezes, and by shared surfaces like door handles and tablets.
Wash with soap and water for about 20 seconds: palms, backs of hands, between fingers, thumbs, and under nails.
Always wash before eating or helping with food, and after the toilet, blowing your nose, touching animals, or coming inside.
Cough and sneeze into your elbow, not your hand, so your hands stay clean for touching things.
topic_content.scenario: Mia pets a neighbour's dog on the walk home, then goes straight to the snack cupboard. What should she do first, and what could happen if she skips it?

topic_content.name: dental care
key_points: Brush twice a day for about two minutes with a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste.
Brush every surface: outsides, insides, and the chewing tops, plus gently along the gum line.
Sugary drinks sipped slowly over a long time give germs more time to harm teeth than the same drink finished quickly.
Adult teeth grow in around this age and do not get replaced, so caring for them matters.
topic_content.scenario: Theo brushes hard and fast for 20 seconds and his gums hurt afterwards. Name two things he could change.

topic_content.name: sleep and rest
key_points: Children this age generally need somewhere around 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night.
Sleep is when the body grows, repairs, and files away what you learned that day.
Screens close to bedtime make it harder to fall asleep because bright light tells the brain it is still daytime.
A steady bedtime and a wind-down routine help more than trying to catch up at the weekend.
topic_content.scenario: Ana feels grumpy and cannot concentrate by mid-morning most days. What sleep questions would help work out why?

topic_content.name: sun and skin care
key_points: Skin can burn on cloudy days and in winter, not just in summer sun.
Sunscreen goes on before going outside and needs putting on again after swimming or a long time outdoors.
Shade, a hat, and covering clothes protect as well as sunscreen does.
Sunburn is an injury to the skin, and it hurts for days after the sun has gone.
topic_content.scenario: A family plans a cloudy afternoon at a lake. Someone says sunscreen is not needed because there is no sun. What would you tell them?

topic_content.name: resting and recovering when sick
key_points: Rest, fluids, and time are what most everyday illnesses need.
Staying home when sick protects other people, and is not something to feel guilty about.
Only a trusted adult gives medicine — never a child, a sibling, or a friend.
Tell an adult about symptoms that get worse, will not stop, or make it hard to breathe.
topic_content.scenario: Jo has a sore throat and a temperature but does not want to miss a school trip. What is the healthy choice here, and who decides?

home_connection: With a guardian, choose one routine step from the card to try this week and talk about what made it easier or harder.
performance_task: Build a personal daily health routine card with morning, daytime, and bedtime steps, and explain what each step protects. No body measurement is used.
adapted_alternative: Any routine step may be described, drawn, sequenced with picture cards, or demonstrated by an adult instead of written. A step a learner cannot do independently is planned as an adult-supported step, which counts fully.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: Household hygiene items only (soap, toothbrush, sunscreen). No specialized equipment.
guardian_safety_review.food_or_allergy_note: Check soap, sanitizer, sunscreen, and toothpaste against any known skin or ingredient allergy before use.

subject: health
title: Food, Water, and Moving My Body
standards: Michigan Health Practice 1: Self-Awareness and Analyzing Influences
Michigan Health Practice 5: Self-Management and Goal Setting
Michigan Health Topic (Grades 3-5): Balanced Eating and Physical Activity
essential_question: How do food, water, and movement give my body energy for the things I want to do?

topic_content.name: variety across food groups
key_points: Different foods do different jobs, so eating a range works better than eating a lot of one thing.
A useful pattern is some fruit or vegetables, some grains, some protein, and some dairy or an alternative.
Foods are not good or bad; foods that are mostly for enjoyment simply fit alongside the rest.
What a family eats depends on culture, budget, and what is available, and all of those are valid.
topic_content.scenario: Two lunches both contain four items. What questions would help you tell whether each one gives a range of foods, without calling either lunch bad?

topic_content.name: food allergies and safe sharing
key_points: A food allergy is the body reacting to a food as if it were dangerous, and it can be serious very fast.
Common ones include peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, wheat, soy, fish, shellfish, and sesame.
Never share or swap food with someone who has an allergy unless a trusted adult has checked it.
Signs to get an adult for immediately: swelling of the face or lips, a rash, trouble breathing, or vomiting after eating.
Wash hands after eating an allergen so it is not left on shared surfaces.
topic_content.scenario: Rae offers half a peanut-butter sandwich to a classmate who says "I think I am allergic to nuts." What is the right move, and who needs to know?

topic_content.name: hunger and fullness signals
key_points: The body sends signals: a rumbling or empty stomach, low energy, or trouble concentrating.
Fullness arrives slowly, so eating at a steady pace helps you notice it.
Being hungry between meals is normal and is what snacks are for.
Different days need different amounts, and that is expected, not a problem to fix.
topic_content.scenario: Kai finishes lunch quickly and still feels hungry, then feels uncomfortably full ten minutes later. What might explain that?

topic_content.name: drinking water through the day
key_points: Water is what the body uses for almost everything, and it is lost through sweat and breathing.
Thirst, a dry mouth, a headache, or dark yellow urine can all mean it is time to drink.
You need more when it is hot and when you have been active.
Water is the everyday drink; sugary drinks are occasional.
topic_content.scenario: After an hour of outdoor play on a hot day, Nico has a headache and has not had a drink. What should happen next?

topic_content.name: everyday movement and active play
key_points: Children this age benefit from around an hour of activity a day, and it does not have to happen all at once.
Movement that counts includes walking, cycling, dancing, chores, and free play, not only sport.
Activity you enjoy is the activity you keep doing.
Movement helps mood and sleep as well as the body.
topic_content.scenario: Someone says they "did no exercise" on a day when they walked to school, helped carry shopping, and danced in the kitchen. What would you point out?

topic_content.name: kitchen and food safety basics
key_points: Wash hands before and after handling food.
Keep raw meat separate from food that will not be cooked, and wash anything it touched.
Cold food belongs in the fridge; food left out for hours is not safe to eat.
Ask an adult before using knives, the hob, the oven, or anything hot.
topic_content.scenario: A chopping board was used for raw chicken and is about to be used for cutting apples. What has to happen first, and why?

home_connection: With a guardian, look at what the household already keeps for quick snacks and talk about which ones travel well.
performance_task: Design flexible fuel-and-move plans for three different kinds of days, including a safe plan for sharing food with someone who has an allergy. No calories, weights, diets, body-size targets, or good-and-bad food labels are used.
adapted_alternative: Plans may use pictures, cut-outs, dictation, or spoken description. Learners with food allergies, medical diets, religious or cultural food practices, or limited food access plan with the foods actually available to them, and the adult may substitute any example.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: Optional clean, empty food packaging. No cooking with heat is required.
guardian_safety_review.environment: Kitchen or table setting with an adult present for any food handling.
guardian_safety_review.movement_hazards: Active-play examples only; the learner chooses intensity and may sit or rest at any point.
guardian_safety_review.food_or_allergy_note: Guardian confirms every food example, tasting, and handling against household allergies, intolerances, and dietary practices. No tasting is required to complete any lesson.

subject: health
title: Feelings, Calm, and Asking for Help
standards: Michigan Health Practice 1: Self-Awareness and Analyzing Influences
Michigan Health Practice 2: Social Awareness, Relationship, and Communication Skills
Michigan Health Topic (Grades 3-5): Mental and Emotional Health
essential_question: How can I notice what I feel and choose a helpful next step?
topics: where feelings show up in the body

topic_content.name: naming feelings
key_points: Naming a feeling accurately makes it easier to handle than calling everything "fine" or "bad".
Useful words include frustrated, disappointed, nervous, embarrassed, lonely, excited, and proud.
Feelings come in sizes: a little annoyed is not the same as furious.
All feelings are allowed. What you do with a feeling is the part you choose.
topic_content.scenario: Ellis snaps at a friend after losing a game. What might Ellis actually be feeling underneath, and what word fits best?

topic_content.name: telling a trusted adult
key_points: A trusted adult is someone who keeps you safe, listens, and takes action — often a parent, carer, teacher, coach, school nurse, or relative.
It helps to have more than one, including one outside your home.
Tell an adult when someone is hurt or unsafe, when something feels wrong, or when a problem is too big to solve alone.
If the first adult does not help, keep telling until someone does. That is not being a nuisance.
Telling to keep someone safe is never the same as tattling to get someone in trouble.
topic_content.scenario: Priya told one adult that something at the park worried her and was told "do not worry about it." She still feels worried. What should Priya do?

topic_content.name: where feelings show up in the body
key_points: Strong feelings often show up physically: a fast heartbeat, a tight chest, hot cheeks, a churning stomach, or tense shoulders.
These signals are early warnings that can be noticed before a feeling gets big.
Bodies differ, so signals are personal and no one signal is the correct one.
Noticing a signal early gives you more choices about what to do next.
topic_content.scenario: Before reading aloud, Devi's hands shake and her stomach churns. What is her body telling her, and what could she do with that information?

topic_content.name: calming and coping tools
key_points: Slow breathing out for longer than you breathe in settles the body down.
Moving, stretching, drinking water, or stepping outside can all help.
Grounding works: name things you can see, hear, and touch right now.
Different tools suit different feelings and places, so having a menu beats having one trick.
topic_content.scenario: A calming tool that works at home is not allowed in the middle of a lesson. What else could work in that setting?

topic_content.name: kindness and empathy
key_points: Empathy is imagining how a situation feels from where someone else is standing.
You can be kind to someone without agreeing with them.
Small actions count: including someone, noticing effort, checking in after a hard day.
Kindness towards yourself matters too, especially after a mistake.
topic_content.scenario: A classmate gets an answer wrong and goes quiet. What could you do that helps without drawing more attention to them?

topic_content.name: big problems and small problems
key_points: Small problems can usually be solved by you, or by waiting, or with a small amount of help.
Big problems involve someone being hurt, unsafe, or scared, and always need an adult.
Sorting the size of a problem helps you pick the right response instead of panicking or ignoring it.
If you are not sure which size it is, treat it as big and ask an adult.
topic_content.scenario: Sort these: a lost pencil; a friend who will not share; someone being threatened. Which need an adult, and which do not?

home_connection: With a guardian, agree on one calm-down option that is allowed at home and one that is allowed away from home.
performance_task: Create a personal calm-down menu, and with a guardian make a trusted-adult contact card the family keeps. The contact card stays with the guardian and is never graded, collected, or stored by the course.
adapted_alternative: Calming tools may be movement-based, still, sensory, verbal, or silent, and each learner picks tools their body and setting allow. Any scenario may be answered by pointing, choosing from options, drawing, or speaking.

guardian_safety_review.environment: Quiet indoor space with a break space available.

subject: health
title: Friends, Boundaries, and Speaking Up
standards: Michigan Health Practice 2: Social Awareness, Relationship, and Communication Skills
Michigan Health Practice 6: Advocacy and Health Promotion
Michigan Health Topic (Grades 3-5): Healthy Relationships
essential_question: How do respectful words and clear boundaries keep me and my friendships safe?
topics: personal body boundaries and unsafe touch

topic_content.name: listening and taking turns
key_points: Listening means letting someone finish, not planning your reply while they talk.
Checking back — "so you mean..." — proves you understood.
Taking turns applies to talking as well as to games.
Interrupting is sometimes necessary, for example when someone is in danger.
topic_content.scenario: Two friends both want to describe their weekend and keep talking over each other. Suggest a rule that would fix it.

topic_content.name: personal body boundaries and unsafe touch
key_points: Your body belongs to you, and you may decide who hugs, tickles, or touches you — including relatives.
The parts covered by a swimsuit are private. Use correct names for them; correct names make it possible to be understood and believed.

No one should look at, touch, photograph, or ask to see your private parts, except a doctor or nurse checking your health with your guardian present, or a carer helping you stay clean when you need help.
You may say no to any touch, even from someone you know and like, and even if you said yes before.
If someone breaks this rule it is never your fault, no matter what they said, gave you, or promised.
Tell a trusted adult straight away, and keep telling until someone helps.
topic_content.scenario: An older cousin keeps tickling Jordan after Jordan says stop, and says "you love it really." Is Jordan allowed to say no? What exactly could Jordan say, and who should Jordan tell?

topic_content.name: asking for and giving permission
key_points: Ask before you touch someone, take their things, or share something about them.
Permission has to be freely given; pestering someone until they give in is not permission.
A yes can be taken back at any time.
When someone says no to you, the respectful answer is to stop and not to argue.
topic_content.scenario: Ben wants a hug from a friend who steps back. What should Ben do, and what should he not do?

topic_content.name: secrets, surprises, and telling
key_points: A surprise is happy and gets told soon, like a birthday present.
A secret you are told to keep forever, especially about touching or about your body, is not safe and should be told.
Adults who ask a child to keep a secret from their guardian are breaking a rule, even if they are known and liked.
Threats and bribes are warning signs, not reasons to stay quiet.
You will not be in trouble for telling.
topic_content.scenario: Someone gives Alex a present and says "this is our secret, do not tell your mum." What kind of secret is that, and what should Alex do?

topic_content.name: making and repairing friendships
key_points: Friendships need shared time, shared interest, and being reliable.
Disagreements are normal and do not have to end a friendship.
A real repair names what you did, says sorry for that specific thing, and changes something.
"Sorry you feel that way" is not an apology.
topic_content.scenario: Rowan broke a promise to a friend. Write what a real apology from Rowan would sound like.

topic_content.name: teasing, bullying, and reporting
key_points: Bullying is deliberate, repeated, and aimed at someone who is finding it hard to stop it.
It can be physical, spoken, social such as deliberate exclusion, or online.
A bystander who tells an adult, includes the person afterwards, or refuses to join in changes the outcome.
Reporting bullying is telling to keep someone safe; it is not tattling.
topic_content.scenario: The same group leaves one classmate out of every game and laughs when they walk past. Is this bullying? What can a bystander do?

home_connection: With a guardian, agree on the family rule for secrets and who is always safe to tell.
performance_task: Practise and write short scripts for asking permission, saying no, and getting help, using fictional situations only.
adapted_alternative: Scripts may be spoken, signed, typed, drawn as a comic, or acted with figures or puppets. Role-play is optional and may always be replaced by describing what a character should say.

guardian_safety_review.food_or_allergy_note: None. This unit covers personal-safety rules; guardians may wish to preview it.

subject: health
title: Staying Safe at Home, Outside, and Online
standards: Michigan Health Practice 4: Decision Making and Problem Solving
Michigan Health Practice 3: Information and Resource Seeking
Michigan Health Topic (Grades 3-5): Safety and Injury Prevention
essential_question: How do I spot a hazard early and choose the safest next step?

topic_content.name: home and kitchen safety
key_points: Common home hazards: wet floors, trailing cables, cluttered stairs, hot drinks, and unlocked cupboards with chemicals.
Hot pan handles turn inwards so they cannot be knocked.
Never put water on a pan fire and never carry a burning pan.
Ask an adult before using anything hot, sharp, or electrical.
topic_content.scenario: Walk through a kitchen where a kettle cable trails over the edge, a pan handle sticks out, and cleaning bottles sit under an open sink. Name each hazard and one fix.

topic_content.name: emergency help and calling 911
key_points: In the United States, call 911 for a real emergency: a fire, someone badly hurt, someone who cannot breathe, or a crime happening now.
Say what happened, where you are including the full address, and your name. Do not hang up until told to.
Learn your home address and a guardian's phone number by heart, and know where the phone is.
Calling 911 as a joke is never safe, because it takes help away from someone who needs it.
Non-emergencies — a scraped knee, a lost pet, a broken window — go to a trusted adult, not to 911.
topic_content.scenario: A neighbour has fallen and cannot get up or reach a phone. Is this a 911 call? Say out loud exactly what you would tell the operator.

topic_content.name: wheels, helmets, and street safety
key_points: A helmet sits level, two fingers above the eyebrows, with the strap snug under the chin.
A helmet that has taken a hard knock is replaced, even if it looks fine.
Cross at crossings, stop at the kerb, look both ways, and make eye contact with drivers.
Headphones and phones make it harder to notice traffic.
topic_content.scenario: A helmet slides back off the forehead and the strap is loose. What needs adjusting before riding?

topic_content.name: water safety
key_points: Never swim alone, and only swim where an adult is watching.
Open water is different from a pool: cold, currents, and hidden depth make it far less predictable.
If someone is in trouble in water, do not go in after them — shout for an adult, and reach or throw something that floats.
Wear a life jacket on boats and in open water, whatever your swimming ability.
topic_content.scenario: A friend has waded out too far in a lake and is struggling. You are a strong swimmer. What do you actually do first?

topic_content.name: fire safety
key_points: Working smoke alarms give the warning; adults test them and change batteries.
If a smoke alarm sounds, get out, stay out, and call for help from outside.
Crawl low under smoke, because the cleanest air is near the floor.
Feel a closed door with the back of your hand before opening it; if it is hot, use another way out.
If clothing catches fire: stop, drop, and roll. Agree a meeting place outside in advance.
topic_content.scenario: The alarm sounds at night and the bedroom door handle feels hot. What is the safe sequence of actions?

topic_content.name: device and online safety basics
key_points: Personal information — full name, address, school, phone number, passwords — stays private online.
People online are not always who they say they are.
Anything sent can be saved and shared onwards, even if it seems to disappear.
If something online is scary, mean, or asks you to keep a secret, tell a trusted adult straight away. You will not be in trouble.
topic_content.scenario: Someone in a game chat says they are also nine, asks which school you go to, and asks you not to tell your parents. What is wrong here, and what do you do?

home_connection: With a guardian, walk the home fire escape route and agree the outside meeting place.
performance_task: Make a household and outdoor safety plan with hazard checks, safe steps, an escape route, and who to contact. A guardian reviews and confirms the plan.
adapted_alternative: A safety walk may be done by an adult with the learner directing from a seated position, by spoken description with no photographs taken, or entirely through a floor-plan drawing. No learner is required to reach, lift, or test any hazard.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: Helmet and protective gear only if the learner uses wheels; smoke alarm and emergency contact list for review by the adult.
guardian_safety_review.environment: Home interior and, if chosen, a guardian-supervised outdoor area. Water and fire content is taught as discussion and planning only.
guardian_safety_review.movement_hazards: A home safety walk involves moving through the home; an adult accompanies the learner. No learner tests, touches, or operates a hazard, alarm, appliance, water source, or flame.
guardian_safety_review.food_or_allergy_note: Kitchen safety discussion may reference household foods; no tasting or cooking is required.

subject: health
title: Good Information and Healthy Choices
standards: Michigan Health Practice 3: Information and Resource Seeking
Michigan Health Practice 4: Decision Making and Problem Solving
Michigan Health Practice 6: Advocacy and Health Promotion
Michigan Health Topic (Grades 3-5): Substance Use and Misuse
Michigan Health Topic (Grades 3-5): Community and Environmental Health
essential_question: How do I find information I can trust and use it to make a healthy choice?

topic_content.name: trusted adults and health helpers
key_points: Health helpers include doctors, nurses, dentists, pharmacists, school nurses, and paramedics.
Different helpers do different jobs, so knowing who to ask saves time.
It is fine to ask a health helper questions about your own body and care.
A trusted adult usually helps you reach the right helper.
topic_content.scenario: Who would you ask about a tooth that hurts when you drink something cold, and who would you ask about a cut that will not stop bleeding?

topic_content.name: medicine and household product safety
key_points: Medicine is given by a trusted adult only — never taken by yourself and never shared with anyone.
Medicine that helps one person can seriously harm another, even at the same age.
Vitamins and sweets can look alike; if you are not certain what something is, do not put it in your mouth.
Cleaning products, vapes, alcohol, and garden chemicals are not for children and are stored away for that reason.
If someone has swallowed something they should not have, tell an adult immediately — speed matters.
topic_content.scenario: A younger sibling finds a bottle of coloured tablets on a low shelf and says they look like sweets. What do you do, in what order?

topic_content.name: reliable information and advertising
key_points: Adverts are made to sell something, so they show the best case, not the whole picture.
Reliable health information usually comes from health organisations, hospitals, and health professionals.
Warning signs: miracle claims, "doctors hate this", pressure to buy now, and no author.
Checking a claim in a second place is the simplest way to test it.
topic_content.scenario: A video says one drink "boosts your immune system instantly" and links to a shop. List two reasons to be suspicious.

topic_content.name: saying no and getting away
key_points: A refusal works better when it is short, clear, and repeated: "No thanks." "I said no."
You do not owe anyone an explanation for a no.
Having an exit ready — leaving, going to an adult, phoning home — matters as much as the words.
Real friends accept a no; pressure to do something unsafe is a signal about them, not about you.
topic_content.scenario: An older child offers Sasha a vape and says everyone does it. Write what Sasha says, and what Sasha does next.

topic_content.name: simple decision steps
key_points: Stop and name the actual choice.
List the options, including the ones nobody mentioned.
Think through what likely happens after each, for you and for others.
Choose, act, and afterwards ask whether it worked.
If the choice involves safety, add an adult to the process.
topic_content.scenario: Friends want to take a shortcut across a building site. Walk through the steps out loud and say what you decide.

topic_content.name: caring for our shared community
key_points: Community health means the conditions everyone shares: clean water, clean air, safe places to play.
Litter, waste, and pollution affect other people and animals, not only the person dropping it.
Children can genuinely change things by asking, writing, organising, and setting an example.
Advocacy means speaking up for something better, with a reason behind it.
topic_content.scenario: A local park has broken glass near the play area. Who could you tell, and what would make the message more likely to work?

home_connection: With a guardian, find out where medicines are stored in your home and why they are kept there.
performance_task: Create a short health advocacy message for family or community, supported by one adult-checked reliable source.
adapted_alternative: The advocacy message may be a poster, a spoken message, a letter, an audio note, a slide, or a described plan. No public posting, publication, or performance is required.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: Medicine and household-product containers are viewed with an adult only, and are never opened, handled, or tasted by the learner.
guardian_safety_review.environment: Indoor setting; supervised internet use if an online source is chosen.
